release.evaluation_role: diagnostic, not blind: Wildcat was the obligations-v3 holdout and motivated parts of v3.1

repair_loop.summary: Zero-asset vault that is still staked to the DSS makes finalizeSlashing revert with ZeroAmount and leaves the healthy vault unslashed; verified end to end.
Changing the allowlisted handler makes a queued NativeVault slash revert with NotSlashStore and restoring it unblocks it, but it requires the trusted manager role so severity is Low/QA at best.
A DSS inflates totalAssets before requestSlashing, redeems its own deposit inside the veto window, and finalizeSlashing then burns 1000 of 1000 honest assets against a 30% cap (300 allowed).

The test proves that an operator who finalizes a pre-scheduled unstake first makes requestSlashing revert with VaultNotStakedToDSS (even against a DSS with all-reverting hooks) and exits with the full 1000, while a control shows the slash lands if requested one second earlier.

The test proves a slash queued while the operator was registered is finalized after it unstaked and unregistered, burning 100 tokens from each vault and cutting a post-unregistration depositor from 1000 to 950; whether that violates the intended invariant remains a design-intent question.

The test proves a queued stake cannot be cancelled, a stranger can finalize it and a registered DSS can then slash the vault from 1000 to 700, but a second test shows the operator can avoid this by unregistering during the 9-day delay, which narrows the claim.

repair_wildcat.summary: A direct call to onQueueWithdrawal by an arbitrary EOA consumes a victim's one-time provider voucher and makes the victim's later (delayed) withdrawal or deposit revert, but only with a stateful short-TTL provider plus a delay past the TTL; the missing hooked-market check is the enabler for known lenders, though the market's onTransfer path can also reach providers for unknown recipients (without harming them).

addRoleProvider(EOA) reverts with empty data in both AccessControlHooks and FixedTermLoanHooks so a non-borrower EOA cannot be a push provider, but the test also shows the borrower EOA or a one-function wrapper contract unblocks lenders, so no loss or DoS follows and the binding-requirement claim is not established from the repo.

After closeMarket() on a fixed-term market the term end is unchanged and lenders cannot queue withdrawals until it elapses (265 days in the test, zero interest meanwhile, full recovery at term end, borrower can release it early), so the behavior is confirmed as a bounded delay with no loss, and no in-repo clause shows it contradicts intended behavior.

A second role provider can take over and then cut another provider's credential from 365 days to 1 hour with two grantRole calls (the direct cut reverts), after which the victim's deposit reverts with NotApprovedLender; the borrower can already block deposits and can restore access in one call.

The test confirms queueing is rejected until fixedTermEndTime and cash arrives one batchDuration later (queue at term end, payout at term end + 1 day), but shows no spec violation or loss (docs say withdrawals are disallowed before term end; payout equals the claim at queue time), so impact is not demonstrated.

The finding's numbers reproduce exactly (0.8005 vs 0.9676), but the extra is lender interest, the configured delinquency fee and protocol fee for the 363 days the batch was unpaid (independent calculation matches to the wei), and funds-first pricing equals an on-time repayment, so the claim of overcharge is not supported (the ordering favors the borrower).

On the unmodified code, in a closed market Alice executes early against a one-member batch, later joiners (Bob's dust requests) lower the batch rate by rounding so payouts exceed batch.normalizedAmountPaid, and Laurence's full executeWithdrawal reverts with an arithmetic underflow even though the market holds the tokens; closeMarket does succeed with the unpaid batch pending because it pays it.

Through a real WildcatMarket deployed via HooksFactory with FixedTermLoanHooks, the borrower cuts APR from 10% to 0% mid-term (and by staged 25% cuts when funds are borrowed) while the lender's queueWithdrawal reverts with WithdrawBeforeTermEnd; the repo's docs do not state that APR changes are prohibited during the term, and Known Issues lists borrower APR reductions as a known malicious-borrower avenue.

setHooksAddress's clear step shr(96, shl(96, x)) keeps bits 96..159 (the low 64 bits of the old address), so setting a second address yields newAddress OR old low 64 bits (e.g. 0x1111...1111 becomes 0x111111111111111111111111BbBbBBbBBBbBBBBb), and via HooksFactory.deployMarketAndHooks a config carrying a stale address makes deployment revert; the only call site takes borrower-supplied input and the top 96 address bits cannot be altered, so impact shown is limited to a failed or misdirected deployment for that borrower.

The test disproves the claim: availableLiquidityForPendingBatch subtracts the normalized amount still owed to older unpaid batches, so a newer batch is paid only from assets in excess of what the older batch needs (nothing when the repayment is smaller than the older debt, only the excess otherwise), and a 1000-run fuzz shows the older batch always ends up paid min(owed, available) with the idle assets reserved for it; the report's cited line WildcatMarketWithdrawals.sol#L153 is only the queueFullWithdrawal doc comment.
